grammar[0].fact: German irony tends to come with a straight face and no warning: *Das hast du ja super gemacht*, after you’ve dropped the cake. The giveaway is the little word *ja*. Listen for it. In praise, it’s rare. In sarcasm, it’s nearly always there.

document.intro: A real playbill for two Vienna theatres, for Wednesday 10 February 1808. Read the two big titles first, then the small notice at the bottom left: someone took the wrong coat at a ball, and the theatre is asking for it back.
document.fact: Long before ads, the theatre bill was the town’s news sheet. Actors who were ill were named at the bottom, as they are here. If you’d wanted a ticket for the masked ball that night, you’d have paid three gulden and could have danced till five.

reading.title: Sehr witzig
reading.intro: Max is English, and he has lived in Germany for some years. He has never quite known when Germans are joking. Tonight Lena has brought him to a small cabaret in a pub cellar. The comedian, Herr Rolle, has noticed him in the front row, and Max has made a mistake: he has laughed first.
reading.fact: German *Kabarett* has a long, political history: it was risky in the 1930s, and sharp in the divided Germany. Its descendants now run on TV in the evening. *Die heute-show*, a satirical news programme, has a very large audience.
